tip: Pop-up headlights and a small oval mouth: the NA is the only MX-5 generation with pop-ups.
Smooth, rounded long-nose body with round tail-light clusters; many carry the tall hoop rear wing.
Squared-off, wedge-like body with four round tail lights, a Skyline hallmark.
Low mid-engined coupé with a cab-forward glasshouse and a full-width rear light bar; pop-up headlights until the 2002 facelift.
Long-nose, short-tail fastback with headlights recessed into the front wings.
Rounded 'bug' shape with no front grille: the air-cooled engine sits at the rear.
Full-width canvas roll-back roof ('an umbrella on wheels'); the bonnet is finely corrugated on cars built before 1960 and has five ribs after.
Streamlined 'spaceship' body riding on hydropneumatic suspension; from late 1967 (1968 model year) four headlamps sit under a smooth glass canopy, the inner pair turning with the steering.
Boxy little two-door with a Duroplast (resin and cotton-fibre) body and a smoky two-stroke engine.
Tiny two-box shape with wheels pushed to the corners and visible external seams down the A-pillars and along the sills. Sold under several badges (Austin, Morris, Rover).
Rear-engined bubble with a fabric sunroof and small round headlamps in a grille-less nose; doors are rear-hinged on 1957–65 cars.
Two-piece split windscreen and a big V-shaped swage line on the nose carrying the VW roundel.
Upward-opening gullwing doors and 'eyebrow' bulges over the wheel arches.
Very long bonnet over a small oval air intake; Series 1 cars (1961–1967) have glass-covered headlamps.
The last air-cooled 911: much more flared wheel arches, smoother front and rear bumpers and teardrop-shaped mirrors compared with earlier 911s.
Extreme flat wedge with scissor doors and NACA ducts cut into the flanks.
Low, sharply faceted V12 wedge that replaced the Murciélago in 2011; the 2017-on Aventador S has a reworked front bumper.
Spartan Pininfarina wedge with Kevlar, carbon-fibre and aluminium panels and plastic windows (the first fifty had sliding Lexan side windows); every F40 left the factory in Rosso Corsa red.
Long bonnet, short deck, a galloping-horse emblem in the grille and triple vertical tail-light bars on each side.
Full-width grille with hidden headlights and a 'coke-bottle' waist. 1968 has an undivided grille, 1969 a centre divider, 1970 a chrome bumper looping around the grille.
Long bonnet and short deck; the 1969 car is more squared-off, with a heavy crease over the wheel arches and dummy vents ahead of the rear wheels.
Wide, recessed full-width grille framing quad round headlights; low, broad E-body proportions.
Flat aluminium panels, exposed door hinges and an upright windscreen: a direct descendant of the Series Land Rovers.
Seven-slot grille with round headlamps and exposed hinges; the JK was the first Wrangler offered with four doors (Unlimited).
Sharp horizontal crease along the flanks at door-handle height and the thick C-pillar every Golf is known for.
Wedge-shaped Kammback profile with a split rear window: a horizontal bar crosses the hatch glass.
No grille at all, slim headlamps in a smooth nose and one continuous sweep of glass roof.
Aluminium-bodied full-size pickup; many trims have C-clamp-shaped LED running lights in the headlamps.
Short, upright two-door body-on-frame 4×4, a little larger than a Jeep CJ, with round headlamps in a flat grille panel; replaced by the 70 Series in most markets in 1984.
Boxy mini 4×4 with upright A-pillars, a flat clamshell bonnet, side windows that dip at the front, roof drip rails and a simple black grille with round headlamps.
Giugiaro's sharp-edged 'folded paper' two-box hatchback with a steep tailgate and round headlamps (rectangular on later US cars).
Boxy, upright body-on-frame 4×4 with flat panels, round headlamps and a spare wheel on the side-hinged rear door; the W463 brought luxury trim to the G in 1990.
Smooth, curvy two-seat coupé with pop-up headlamps; the last RX-7, with a sequential twin-turbo rotary engine.
Wide, flat Pininfarina wedge with long horizontal 'cheese-grater' strakes running from the doors into the rear wings.
Low, curvaceous Gandini body with the engine behind the cabin; pre-SV cars have black 'eyelashes' around the headlamps.
Porsche's first production car: a small, rounded rear-engined coupé or convertible whose shape stayed largely unchanged from 1948 to 1965.
Sharp-edged Sting Ray body with hidden headlamps in rotating housings; the 1963 coupé alone has the split rear window.
Upright, boxy little car with a top-hinged one-piece tailgate (often called the first mass-produced hatchback) and a full-width body roomier than the 2CV's.

Upright, square-cut saloon with horizontal headlamps, wide ribbed tail-lights and indicators on the outer edges of the front; round-lamp fronts on lower models until 1983 (and in North America), rectangular lamps otherwise.
Short, wide E-body pony car that shares its platform but no sheet metal with the Dodge Challenger: two headlamps instead of the Challenger's four (only the 1971 Barracuda had four).

Flat-panelled utility 4×4 with headlamps in the front wings and a plastic grille (earlier Series cars had a metal one); the most common Series Land Rover, built 1971–1985 before the coil-sprung 90/110 (later Defender).

Twelfth-generation Corolla (2018 on), sold as a hatchback (Corolla Sport, or Auris in some early markets), saloon and Touring Sports estate; some markets get a different 'Prestige' saloon front borrowed from the Camry.
Kinetic-design Focus with a trapezoidal grille; the 2014 facelift (Mk 3.5) brought thinner, sharper headlamps and the wide Aston-style grille.
Fifth-generation Polo (2009–2017 in Europe; still built in South Africa as the Polo Vivo); a long-wheelbase saloon was sold in emerging markets as the Vento or Polo Sedan.
BMW-era Mini Hatch, third generation (2014–2024, built at Oxford), with big oval headlamps and a hexagonal grille; renamed Mini Cooper for the 2024 fourth generation.
First-generation Leaf (2010–2017), the world's first series-produced battery-electric car: rounded hatchback with tall, swept-back headlamps and the charging port under a flap in the nose.
Fifth-generation RAV4 (unveiled 2018), styled after the FT-AC concept: angular, truck-like front with an octagonal grille, on the TNGA-K platform shared with the Camry.

First-generation Evoque (L538, 2011–2018), developed from the LRX concept, sold as three- and five-door SUVs and later a convertible; China's Landwind X7 copied its design so closely that a court banned it in 2019.
Tenth and final Lancer Evolution (2007–2016): a four-door saloon with a big trapezoidal 'jet fighter' grille mouth, bonnet vents and four-wheel drive with a 2-litre turbo.
Crisp, small hatchback launched in 1983 to replace the 104 and Talbot Samba; CAR magazine named it 'car of the decade' in 1990. The front has a slatted grille between square headlamps.
Second-generation 3 Series (1982–1994), very like the twin-headlight E21 it replaced; the first 3 Series offered as a four-door and an estate (Touring).
Upright executive saloon (also estate, coupé and cabriolet) built 1984–1997, marketed as the E-Class from 1993; it followed the W123 and was replaced by the W210.
First-generation TT (Type 8N, 1998–2006): a rounded, arch-on-arch coupé or roadster designed by J Mays and Freeman Thomas, built on the Golf Mk4 platform.
Front-mid-engined two-seat roadster launched in 1999 for Honda's 50th anniversary: long bonnet, short tail and swept-back headlamps; the facelifted AP2 looks almost the same as the AP1.

Second-generation 300ZX (Z32), driven up-market from the Z31: wide, low wedge with steeply raked, fixed headlamps and a full-width tail-light bar; sold in the US until 1996 and as the Fairlady Z in Japan.
V10 successor to the Gallardo (2014–2024): a low, faceted wedge with hexagonal themes and Y-shaped daytime lamps, smaller and lower than the V12 Aventador.
Mid-engined V8 Ferrari (2009–2015) that replaced the F430: long, swept headlamps reaching back along the wings and a wide mouth with small winglets; succeeded by the 488.
Volkswagen-era Bugatti hypercar (2005–2015): rounded body, often two-tone, with the horseshoe grille and a big air scoop behind the cabin.
Second-generation Viper (SR II, 1996–2002): long, curvy V10 sports car, sold as the double-bubble GTS coupé and the RT/10 roadster, often with twin stripes over the top.
Third-generation Corvette (1968–1982), patterned on the Mako Shark II concept: long, pinched 'coke-bottle' waist, pop-up headlamps and high, curved front wings.
Sixth-generation Mustang (S550, 2015–2023), the first sold globally: a wide trapezoidal grille with the running-horse badge, slim swept headlamps and three-bar tail lamps.
Sixth-generation Camaro (2016 model year until production ended in December 2023), on GM's Alpha platform: low, slit-like glasshouse and a thin upper grille over a big lower intake.
Retro full-size muscle car (2008–2023) styled after the 1970 Challenger R/T: quad round headlamps set in a wide, recessed grille, built on a shortened LX platform.
Tri-Five Chevrolet (1955–1957) in top Bel Air trim, here the 1957: restrained tail fins, lots of chrome and a wide, full-width front bumper and grille.

The first mass-affordable car (1908–1927), the 'Tin Lizzie': tall, upright and spindly, with thin wooden-spoked wheels, a flat upright radiator and separate mudguards; named most influential car of the 20th century.

Original 'Classic' Saab 900 (1978–1993), based on the Saab 99 but with a longer nose: a sharply wrapped, almost vertical windscreen and a long, rounded body sold as a hatchback, saloon and convertible.

First-generation Delta (1979–1994); the rally-bred HF Integrale shown here has bulged wheel arches, a louvred bonnet and quad round headlamps. It won six consecutive World Rally Constructors' titles (1987–1992).
Touring Superleggera-designed grand tourer (1963–1965), an evolution of the last DB4: the classic Aston grille shape and faired-in headlamps; best known as James Bond's car.

The first Range Rover (1970–1996): a tall, flat-sided box with a clamshell bonnet, a thin 'floating' roof over big glass and round headlamps; two-door only until a four-door joined in 1981, and from 1986 the grille gained horizontal plastic slats.

Toyota's workhorse Land Cruiser since 1984, replacing the 40 Series: a more angular, slab-sided body with a flat bonnet and upright windscreen, sold as short and long wheelbase wagons, the Troop Carrier and the 79 pickup.

First-generation Smart (W450, 1998–2007), a two-seat, rear-engined one-box city car built at Hambach: a tiny tall body with the steel Tridion safety cell exposed in a contrasting colour and bolt-on plastic panels.

The egg-shaped bubble car: one door that is the whole front of the car (the steering wheel swings out with it), a single bench seat and a one-cylinder BMW motorcycle engine; BMW built it under licence from Iso from April 1955 to May 1962.

AMC-designed compact Jeep (1984–2001 in the US): a squared-off, flat-roof box that was the first unibody American off-roader, with a vertical-slot grille between rectangular headlamps and black lower cladding.

Civilian version of AM General's M998 Humvee, sold 1992–2006: enormously wide (86.5 in, to run in tank tracks), flat-sided and slab-bonneted, with a vertical-slot grille between round headlamps and a tall ground clearance; later renamed H1 when the H2 arrived.

Giugiaro-designed wedge with gull-wing doors and unpainted brushed stainless-steel panels, built at Dunmurry in Northern Ireland from 1981 to 1983; louvred rear window, PRV V6 in the back, and the Back to the Future time machine.

Fourth-generation MX-5 (ND, built in Hiroshima since 2015): shorter and about 100 kg lighter than the NC, with a low, wide mouth, slit-like LED headlamps and sharply creased wings; the RF has a fastback targa roof.

Seventh-generation 911 (991, 2011–2019) on an all-new platform: longer wheelbase than the 997, slimmer LED-edged headlamps, a thin full-width rear light strip on later cars and the classic sloping fastback.

The first turbocharged 911 (1975–1989), Porsche's top model throughout: impact-bumper G-body with much wider flared rear arches over fat wheels and the big 'whale tail' (later 'tea-tray') rear spoiler.

Audi's four-wheel-drive turbo coupé (1980–1991) that rewrote rallying: the boxy Audi Coupé shape with Martin Smith's squared-off flared wheel arches, a flat rear spoiler lip and four-ring decals on the doors.
2CV-based open utility (1968–1988) with ribbed ABS plastic body panels, a flat bonnet, a square grille, optional doors and a fold-down fabric top; a four-wheel-drive version ran 1980–1983.

Pelle Petterson-styled 2+2 (1961–1973), first built by Jensen: a long bonnet, egg-crate grille, a dipped chrome side crease and small rear fins; the glass-tailgate 1800ES shooting brake came in 1972. The Saint drove one.

Porsche's first mid-engined roadster since the 914 (986, late 1996–2004): a short two-seater with a fabric top, the same bonnet, wings and 'fried egg' teardrop headlamps as the 996-generation 911, and air intakes ahead of the rear wheels.

BMW's 1995–2002 two-seater on a shortened E36 platform, sold as a roadster (E36/7) and as the 'clown shoe' shooting-brake coupé (E36/8): a long bonnet, kidney grille set low between slanted headlamps, and gill-like side vents behind the front wheels.

Jaguar's first post-war sports car (1948–1954), once the world's fastest production car: a long, flowing body with a narrow vertical-bar oval grille, separate headlamp pods on the wings, faired-in rear wheels and a split windscreen on the open two-seater.

The best-known 'Big Healey' (1959–1967), bodied by Jensen and built at Abingdon: a low, long-bonneted roadster with a wide oval grille of vertical bars, a bonnet scoop and a sweeping two-tone side flash.

Karmann-restyled successor to the TR5 (September 1968 – July 1976): a squared-off, flat-decked roadster with a full-width black grille between the round headlamps and a cut-off Kamm tail, on the older TR chassis.

Volvo's tall-bodied family car of 1956–1970 (sold as the 121/122S): rounded, slightly American-influenced styling with a twin-section grille, a pronounced side crease and small tail fins; two- and four-door saloons and an estate.

Beetle-based 2+2 coupé and convertible (Type 14, 1955–1975) styled by Ghia and hand-built by Karmann: a low, rounded body with a sloping nose, small chrome-slatted 'nostril' grilles either side of the badge and no radiator grille.

Second-generation VW bus (built in Germany late 1967–1979, much longer in Mexico and Brazil): a one-piece curved 'bay window' windscreen replacing the T1's split screen, a big VW roundel on the flat nose and, on later T2b vans, the indicators moved up beside the fresh-air grille.

The first mass-produced front-wheel-drive, unit-bodied car (Citroën, 1934–1957): long and low for its day with no running boards, separate flowing front wings, free-standing headlamps and a tall grille carrying the double-chevron logo.

Hethel-built mid-engined wedge (1976–2004), one of Giugiaro's 'folded paper' designs: a flat, knife-edged nose, a steeply raked windscreen and a louvred engine cover; Peter Stevens softened the lines for the 1987 X180 cars.

Heavily revised 348 (May 1994–1999) with Pininfarina's wind-tunnel-shaped body: a wide oval front intake under pop-up headlamps, big side intakes, four round tail lamps under a mesh grille and a flat underbody.
Replaced the 650S in 2017 on the MonoCage II carbon tub: dihedral doors, a teardrop canopy and hollow 'eye socket' headlamp pods that duct air to the radiators; no side intakes behind the doors.
Audi's Gallardo-based mid-engined supercar (June 2006 – August 2015): a large single-frame grille, LED-lined headlamps and the contrasting 'sideblade' panel behind the doors (absent on the Spyder).
Lamborghini's first SUV under Volkswagen (December 2017, 2018 model year) on the MLB Evo platform: a coupé-like five-door with a sharply sloping roof, hexagonal arches and Y-shaped light signatures.

Sixth-generation Z car (2008–2020, Fairlady Z Z34 in Japan): a short, wide two-seater with boomerang-shaped headlamps and tail lamps, a vertical 'fang' of daytime lights in the bumper and a fastback roof; also a roadster.

The 1989–1994 BNR32 revived the GT-R name and won Group A touring-car titles ('Godzilla'): a compact, boxy two-door with slim horizontal headlamps, a thin slatted grille, a bonnet with a slight bulge and a rear wing.
Rotary-engined successor to the RX-7 (2003–2012): a four-seat coupé with rear-hinged 'freestyle' back doors and no B-pillar, flared front wings with a vertical side vent, and pentagonal grille.

Subaru's half of the jointly developed Toyota 86 twin, a front-engined 2+2 fastback built at Ōta, Gunma with a low flat-four boxer: a long bonnet with a low hexagonal Subaru grille, swept headlamps and a short tail; the second generation (ZD8) arrived for 2021–22.

Fifth-generation GR Supra (2019 on), co-developed with BMW alongside the Z4 and built by Magna Steyr in Graz: a short, wide double-bubble-roof coupé with a pointed nose, slim headlamps above deep corner intakes and a ducktail.

Tesla's Model S-based crossover (2015–2026) with falcon-wing rear doors: a smooth, grille-less nose with a small T badge, a huge windscreen sweeping back over the front seats and a rounded, tall fastback rear.

Second-generation Chevelle (1968–1972): an all-new sculpted body with tapered front wings, a long-bonnet/short-deck profile and a high rear deck; the 1970 restyle added a coke-bottle waist and quad headlamps set into a full-width grille, often with SS stripes on the bonnet.

Giugiaro's Bertone coupé on the 105-series Giulia (first shown 1963): a crisp 2+2 with a shield-shaped Alfa grille between twin round lamps, a slim pillared glasshouse and, on early cars, the 'step-nose' (scalino) lip at the front of the bonnet.

Pininfarina-designed and -built roadster (1966–1985): a clean, low body with twin round headlamps in shallow recesses, a slim horizontal grille, twin bonnet power bulges on later cars and, on US cars, big black impact bumpers.

The original Renault 5 (1972–1985, 'Le Car' in the US): a short, upright three-door hatchback with wrap-around plastic bumpers, a flat bonnet with the diamond badge, rectangular headlamps and tall vertical tail lamps beside the hatch.

Third-generation Octavia (Typ 5E, revealed December 2012): a crisply creased liftback or Combi estate with a vertical-slat Škoda grille; the 2017 facelift split each headlamp in two, like a pre-facelift Mercedes E-Class.

Hyundai's first E-GMP electric car (2021 on), inspired by the 1975 Pony: a boxy, flat-sided crossover-hatchback with a full-width clamshell bonnet, square 'Parametric Pixel' lamps and a sharp Z-shaped crease in the doors.

Tesla's compact crossover (2020 on), the best-selling EV ever: a tall, rounded Model 3-like fastback with no grille; the January 2025 'Juniper' refresh added a full-width light bar across the nose and tail.

Eighth-generation Camry (XV70, June 2017 – October 2024) on the TNGA platform: lower and wider, with a huge lower grille opening below a thin upper slot and the Toyota badge, slim swept headlamps and, on sportier trims, a black 'fang' bumper.

Volkswagen's 2011–2023 city car (twin of the SEAT Mii and Škoda Citigo): a tiny, upright hatchback with wheels pushed to the corners, a black-glass tailgate and, before the 2016 facelift, a smiley black bumper band across the nose.

Renault's Clio-based electric supermini (December 2012 – March 2024): a rounded five-door with a big diamond badge hiding the charge port, blue-tinted headlamps on early cars and 'boomerang' lamps after the 2019 facelift.

BMW's first mass-produced electric car (2013–2022), with a carbon-fibre passenger cell: a tall, short city car with rear-hinged coach doors, a black 'stream-flow' band from bonnet to roof and tailgate, and blue-trimmed closed kidney grille.
The Diablo's successor (2001–2010) and Lamborghini's V12 flagship of the decade: scissor doors, a low wedge with angular headlamps, and big air scoops on the rear haunches that open out at speed.

Lamborghini's V10 'baby' (2003–2013), its best seller at the time under Audi: smaller and more compact than the V12 cars, with conventional doors, slim angular headlamps and side intakes behind the doors.

Countach successor (1990–2001) and the first production Lamborghini to exceed 200 mph: a long, smooth wedge with scissor doors, pop-up headlamps on early cars (fixed lamps from 1999) and side air intakes behind the doors.

Named after Ferrari's founder and built with Formula One technology (2002–2004): a carbon-fibre body with an F1-style pointed nose, butterfly doors, big side intakes and a cockpit that tapers to a narrow tail.
Ferrari's hybrid hypercar (project F150, coupé 2013–2016, Aperta roadster after): a low, swoopy body with a black canopy, a deep central nose 'fin', narrow swept headlamps and hollow side channels.
Update of the 360 (2004–2009): the same mid-engined V8 shape, but with two large oval intakes in the nose (inspired by the 1961 Sharknose racer) and bigger, round twin tail lamps.

Pininfarina-styled V8 (1999–2004) with an aluminium frame: rounded, smooth lines that dropped the 1990s sharp edges and pop-up lamps, teardrop headlamps and two separate intakes in the nose, plus a glass engine cover.
Front-engined V12 two-seater that replaced the 575M (2006–2012): a long bonnet with a wide, slatted egg-crate grille, tall vertical headlamps, and 'flying buttresses' behind the cabin.
Veyron successor (shown March 2016, production ended May 2024): a horseshoe grille, four-element LED headlamps and a sweeping C-shaped line that curves along each flank around the doors.

Mercedes-Benz/McLaren grand tourer (2003–2010): a very long bonnet with an F1-style pointed nose and twin headlamps, butterfly doors, and exhausts exiting on the sides behind the front wheels because the flat underbody left no room.

Limited-production plug-in-hybrid hypercar (September 2013 – June 2015): a low open two-seater with a removable roof, vertically stacked LED headlamps and high-mounted 'top pipe' exhausts behind the seats.
Mid-engined V10 roadster (2003–2006), Sports Car International's top car of the 2000s: long, low, removable roof panels, twin-element headlamps, large intakes behind the doors and a rising rear wing.

Limited-production targa two-seater (1995–1997) with a V12 developed from Ferrari's 1990 F1 engine: a curvy body with a big fixed rear wing, round headlamps under clear covers and deep nostril-like bonnet vents.

Homologation version of the 308 GTB (1984–1987): the 308's shape widened with flared wheel arches, a deeper nose with twin driving lamps, longer wheelbase and three slanted vents behind the rear wheels.

Gordon Murray's road car (1992–1998, 106 built), the first production car with a carbon-fibre monocoque and a central driving seat: a compact, rounded body with a roof scoop, small round lamps and upward-opening dihedral doors.
BMW's mid-engined homologation special (E26, 1978–1981) with a Giugiaro glass-fibre body: a sharp wedge with pop-up headlamps, twin small kidneys low in the nose and louvres over the rear window.

The Fiat 500's rear-engined successor (October 1972 – 2000, built for decades in Poland as the 126p 'Maluch'): a tiny, boxy four-seater with flat panels, a plain nose with a chrome or plastic strip, and louvres on the rear engine lid.

AvtoVAZ's first car (1970, sold until 1988 at home), a toughened licence-built Fiat 124: a plain, square three-box saloon with single round headlamps in a full-width chrome grille and thin chrome bumpers. The later 2103/2106 have twin headlamps.

AvtoVAZ's off-roader built since 1977, the first mass-produced 4×4 with a unibody: a short, square three-door box with round headlamps, a wide flat grille, and tail lamps in the rear corners above a high bumper.

Retro-styled compact on the Golf IV platform (launched 1997 for 1998, facelifted 2005, built until 2011): a bubble of three arcs — rounded wings, a domed roof and round headlamps — with the engine in the front, unlike the original.

BMW's plug-in-hybrid sports car (June 2014 – June 2020, roadster from 2018): a very low, layered body with butterfly doors, slim blue-accented kidney grilles, floating 'stream flow' panels over the rear wheels and U-shaped tail lamps.

Tesla's electric pickup, built since 2023: an angular, 'low-polygon' body of flat unpainted stainless-steel panels, a single full-width light bar across the nose and a steeply sloped roof over the covered bed.

Porsche's front-engined V8 grand tourer (1977–1995), 1978 European Car of the Year: a smooth, rounded 2+2 hatchback with headlamps that fold flat to face the sky when off, body-colour bumpers and a big glass rear hatch.

Front-engined four-cylinder sports car on the 924's platform (1982–1991), over 163,000 built: the 924 shape with pumped-out, flared wheel arches, pop-up headlamps and a large curved glass hatch with a rubber spoiler.
